title: Warsh's Fed to Cut Back Rate-Decision Meetings, Escalating Market Suspense
snippet: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh announced the central bank will reduce its rate-setting decisions starting in 2027, raising the stakes for Wall Street amid an already tight-lipped policy era.
content:
Wall Street is bracing for a new era of central bank unpredictability after Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh announced that the central bank will reduce the number of interest rate decisions on its calendar starting in 2027.

Speaking at the conclusion of Wednesday's policy meeting—where officials held interest rates steady despite two dissenting votes calling for a hike—Warsh revealed that 2027 will feature one fewer rate decision. The schedule could be trimmed even further in 2028 to just six rate-setting announcements per year. While scheduled meetings will remain on the calendar, non-decision gatherings will focus instead on broader, long-term monetary policy topics.

Refocusing on Big-Picture Strategy

Warsh framed the schedule change as a deliberate move to give policymakers breathing room to tackle structural economic challenges rather than reacting constantly to short-term data.

The goal is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons," Warsh said during his Wednesday press conference.

The Death of Forward Guidance

The reduction in decision-making meetings compounds a growing sense of anxiety among investors. Since taking the helm, Warsh has systematically dismantled the Fed's traditional communication channels, leaving markets with far less visibility into the central bank's inner workings.

Earlier this year, Warsh put an end to the practice of providing forward guidance—a tool his predecessors used for over a decade to signal upcoming rate moves. "I don't believe in forward guidance," Warsh reiterated on Wednesday. Additionally, the chair has opted out of contributing to the Fed's quarterly "dot plot," which maps out individual policymakers' expectations for short-term rates.

With fewer rate calls on the horizon and virtually no forward-looking cues from the chairman, each remaining meeting will carry vastly higher stakes, potentially introducing higher levels of volatility to global financial markets.
